summary: Presents the Generic Multi-Access encapsulation protocol, which lets a device combine several networks, such as Wi-Fi, LTE, 5G and DSL, below the transport layer. It adds control information such as a sequence number to each packet. It is aimed at applications that have no built-in multipath support. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone uses Wi-Fi and cell data together, like carrying water in two buckets, without the app noticing.

questions: combine wifi and lte below transport layer
subtitle: Lightweight protocol for combining multiple networks below the transport layer

tldr.problem: Devices can connect to multiple networks (Wi-Fi, LTE, 5G, DSL) simultaneously, but applications that lack built-in multipath support cannot use this to improve quality. Existing protocols like GRE add too much overhead.
tldr.mechanism: GMA provides three lightweight encapsulation methods to combine multiple network paths at the convergence layer, adding control information like sequence numbers, timestamps and connection IDs to each packet.
tldr.outcome: Applications can seamlessly benefit from multiple simultaneous connections without modification. Smaller overhead than GRE (especially for trailer-based IP encapsulation) enables more efficient use of diverse access links. It is experimental.

today: RFC 9188 defines an experimental encapsulation protocol. It is not yet a standard, but implementations are being developed to test the protocol's effectiveness and to determine which of the three encapsulation methods are most useful in practice.

sections.title: The Multi-Access Problem
sections.content:
Modern devices often have multiple network interfaces: Wi-Fi, LTE, 5G, DSL, and so on. A smartphone might be connected to Wi-Fi and cell data at the same time. However, most applications are built to use a single path at a time. If the application is not aware of multipath capabilities, it cannot benefit from the combined bandwidth or reliability of multiple links.

GMA (Generic Multi-Access) encapsulation protocol provides a solution by operating at the convergence layer, below the transport layer. It acts as a middleman between the application's packets and the individual network paths, adding control information such as sequence numbers to enable features like packet reordering, retransmission, and load balancing.

The key advantage over existing solutions like GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation) is lower overhead, especially for small packets. GRE requires IP-over-IP tunneling, adding 20 bytes. GMA's trailer-based IP encapsulation adds only 3 bytes minimum, and header-based methods avoid the tunneling overhead entirely.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of building multipath support into every app, GMA does it in the network layer itself. Apps do not need to change; they just get faster and more reliable connections automatically.

sections.title: Protocol Architecture and Use Case
sections.content:
GMA uses a convergence-layer and adaptation-layer architecture. The convergence layer sits above multiple adaptation layers (one per network path). When an IP packet arrives, the convergence layer can decide how to split, aggregate, or duplicate it across the available paths, adding the necessary control information.

Typical use cases include:

  • Multi-path aggregation: A single TCP flow uses the combined bandwidth of Wi-Fi and LTE.
  • Packet duplication: Critical packets are sent over multiple paths for low latency and high reliability.
  • Loss recovery: Lost packets are retransmitted using control information in the GMA header.
  • Concatenation: Small packets are bundled to reduce per-packet overhead.

The protocol is designed for two endpoints that have been pre-configured to use GMA. Configuration can happen through control messages, such as the Multi-Access Management Services (MAMS) protocol, or through pre-loaded settings.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a postal system that can send the same letter via different routes and reassemble it at the destination. It keeps track of pieces with sequence numbers and reorders them if they arrive out of order.

sections.title: Encapsulation Methods
sections.content:
GMA defines three encapsulation methods. Trailer-based IP encapsulation appends a GMA trailer after the IP payload, changing the IP protocol type to 114. The trailer contains optional control fields as needed (checksum, sequence numbers, timestamps, etc.), keeping the minimum overhead to 3 bytes (Next Header and Flags).

Header-based IP encapsulation inserts a GMA header immediately after the IP header. The Flags field comes first so the receiver can determine the header length and decode optional fields. This method is used when trailer-based is not supported.

Header-based non-IP encapsulation uses UDP tunneling and wraps the original IP packet inside. The GMA header sits between the UDP header and the original IP packet. This method is required for IPv6 packets.

The choice of method is negotiated between endpoints. The trailer-based method is preferred for IPv4 when supported, as it avoids IP-over-IP overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: GMA has three ways to add labels to packets: stick a label on the back (trailer), stick a label on the front (header), or wrap it in a box (UDP). Devices agree upfront which method to use.

sections.title: Fragmentation and Concatenation
sections.content:
GMA provides fragmentation for packets that exceed the MTU of a delivery path. Unlike IP fragmentation, GMA fragmentation uses fragment numbers instead of byte offsets, allowing a maximum of 128 fragments per packet. The Fragmentation Control (FC) field carries the More Fragment flag and fragment offset.

GMA also supports concatenation, allowing multiple small IP packets to be bundled into a single GMA PDU. This reduces per-packet overhead for protocols that generate many small packets, such as TCP ACKs. The First SDU Length (FSL) field indicates the boundary between concatenated packets.

Fragmentation and concatenation MUST NOT be performed on the same PDU. The Flow Sequence Number (Flow SN) field, present in most variants, enables the receiver to reorder fragments and detect missing packets.
sections.plainLanguage: If a packet is too big for a path, GMA splits it into numbered pieces. If packets are tiny, GMA bundles several together to save space. The receiver puts the pieces back together in the right order.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
GMA itself does not provide security. It is a zero-hop protocol that relies on the underlying network paths for security. Deployers MUST use additional security protocols like IPsec or DTLS at the adaptation layer when security cannot be guaranteed by the network.

The protocol uses IP protocol type 114 ('Any 0-Hop Protocol'), which is being reused in this experiment. As part of the experiment, GMA endpoints should detect non-GMA uses of protocol 114 and log errors (rate-limited). If a conflict is detected, they should switch to non-IP (UDP) encapsulation.

Local-only packet leak prevention is important: GMA packets have TTL set to 1 to prevent them from escaping beyond the immediate link.
sections.plainLanguage: GMA does not encrypt or sign packets; that is done by layers above and below it. Also, the protocol watches for conflicts with other uses of the same protocol number and can switch to a backup method if needed.
